notesStmt.note: An early draft of lines for this poem (uva.00268) is written on the reverse of a letter to Whitman dated 14 August 1889. In his notes of a visit to the poet on 26 February 1890, Horace Traubel writes that Whitman reported "having sent 'A Twilight Song' to the Century." (See With Walt Whitman in Camden [Carbondale and Edwardsville: Southern Illinois University Press, 1982] 6:311). Therefore, the current manuscript must have been created between these two dates.

The poem represented by this draft was published as "A Twilight Song: For unknown buried soldiers, North and South" in the May 1890 issue of Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine. With minor changes and without the subtitle, it was included in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891) and in the "Good-Bye My Fancy" annex to Leaves of Grass (1891-1892).

lg.l:
As I sit silent ‸in the twilight by the flickering of
oak⹀flame

Musing on long-past war⹀days and ‸of many, a and many a slain, and
buried, long-crumbled dead soldier

Of The truce after the battle, and —and the burial squads,
and the hasty trench
Belonging as ye ‸all are, death's of slaughter's , mystery's

The intangible, the faded out, the vacant
air's, the sands', the unindented seas',

l.del: Or Northern, Southern, East or West,

lg.l: In the shadows and the ‸silent play flickering flames

The The
The
spectral armies moving, by and by ranks on
on ranks on⹀filing,
The mystic roll from all America, ‸or Northern, Southern, East or West,

From wooded Maine, New England's farms,
from fertile Pennsylvania,

The boundless West, the South, the
Caralinas, Texas,

A Ye
million hidden untold
names, left blank, unknown

I put ye in deep within
my thought recorded
